case_name: Direk v. Attorney General of Ontario
text:
CITATION
: Direk v.
Attorney General of Ontario 2013 ONSC 5940

COURT FILE NO.:

CV-09-386582

DATE:

20130920

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE – ONTARIO

RE:

URAL DIREK, Ertug Direkoglu
, KEMAL
DIREKOGLU, and ELIF DIREKOGLU, Applicants/Respondents

AND:

ATTORNEY
GENERAL OF ONTARIO
and
the
Toronto police services board
, Respondents/Moving Parties

BEFORE:
Stinson
J.

COUNSEL:
Ural Direk and Kemal
Direkoglu, acting in person

No one appears on behalf of Ertug Direkoglu
and Elif Direkoglu

Josh Hunter
, for the respondent/moving
party Attorney General of Ontario

Ansuya Pachai
,
for the respondent/moving party the Toronto Police Services Board

HEARD:
July
3, 2013

ENDORSEMENT

[
1
]

This endorsement concerns two motions under Rule
21, one by the respondent Attorney General of Ontario (the "AGO”) and one
by the respondent the Toronto Police Services Board (the "TPSB”). They
were heard together.

[
2
]

The responding parties (the applicants in this
proceeding, collectively "the Direks") are all self-represented. Ural
Direk ("Ural")
,
and his
son Kemal Direkoglu ("Kemal") appeared on their own behalves on the argument of the motion, as they have throughout
this litigation. Their co-applicants, Kemal's brother Ertug Direkoglu ("Ertug")
and his sister Elif Direkoglu "Elif" did not appear.

[
3
]

In essence, the moving parties seek to have this
application stayed or dismissed on the ground that it is frivolous, vexatious
and an abuse of the process of the court. A number of other grounds were
articulated in the notices of motion served by the moving parties (such as
failure to plead all elements of certain causes of action), but in my view, the
motions come to be determined on the former ground.

background

[
4
]

This application is one of numerous proceedings
in which the Direks are or have been involved in the courts of this province.
By their count, the Direks have "over 120 Canadian legal-matters." The
present proceeding was commenced in response to an application initiated in
early 2009 by the AGO in Court File No. CV-09-371609 (the "AGO Application").
The AGO Application was brought under the
Civil Remedies Act,
2001, S.O.
2001, c. 28 seeking the forfeiture of certain property as proceeds or
instruments of crime. The property in question is $229,345 in Canadian currency
and a 2006 Lincoln Mark LT Truck. According to the evidence filed on the AGO Application,
the cash and truck were seized by the police on October 22, 2006 in connection
with their investigation of an alleged illegal drug distribution operation
involving Ertug. The truck was seized from a hotel parking lot following police
surveillance of a hotel room in which Ertug is alleged to have been engaged in
drug trafficking. Ertug was arrested and prosecuted. The cash was found and
seized during a subsequent search of the Direks’ house, carried out pursuant to
a search warrant.

[
5
]

The AGO Application first came before me on
November 6, 2009, when the AGO sought an order that the cash and truck be
forfeited to the Crown under the
Civil Remedies Act
. Although neither
Ertug nor his co-respondent to the AGO Application, Angela Calce (who were both
listed as respondents on the Notice of Application in that proceeding) appeared
on that occasion; however, Ural and Kemal did. In
advance of that date, Ural and Kemal had commenced and
served this application, which is, in effect, a counter-application on behalf of the Direks
and Ismet Direkoglu against the AGO and the TPSB, in
Court File No. CV-09-386582 (the "Direks' Counter-Application"). The Direks' Counter-Application
also came before me on November 6, 2009.

[
6
]

The relief sought in the Direks' Counter-Application
is as follows:

(a)

an order quashing the AGO application;

(b)

"an Order granting leave to the [Direks] to
file after the November 6, 2009 hearing voluminous supplemental materials";

(c)

"an Order granting a six month incessant
initial-continuation of the Friday, November 6, 2009 hearing";

(d)

"an Order granting, if required, an
additional-continuation of the November 6, 2009 hearing";

(e)

"an Order granting an award of
$4,000,000,000.00 ($4 Billion Dollars) in monetary compensation to the [Direks]";

(f)

"an Order rendering all legislative
provisions and Rules of (Common) Law of which the Applicants intend to question
on this very Application the constitutional validity and applicability,
inclusive of such Canadian Laws specified herein, to be constitutionally
inapplicable to the [Direks] over 21 year-long legal matter and
constitutionally invalid";

(g)

costs.

[
7
]

The grounds set out for the Direks' Counter-Application
are lengthy, running to some 17 single spaced pages. I will quote verbatim grounds
A, B, and C from their notice of application:

A.        The belowmentioned Crimes have been, against the Appellant
and his Family, committed as part of an over 21 year-long Canadian
Judiciary-Driven Systematic-Crime ("Systematic-Crime"), an over 21
year-long

Canadian Judiciary-Driven Gross-Systemic
Chain Conspiracy

(''Gross-Systemic
Chain Conspiracy
"), an over 21 year-long Canadian
Judiciary-Driven

Systematic-
Corruption of the State

("Systematic-
Corruption of the State
"), an over 21 year-long
Canadian Judiciary-Driven Systematic-
Crimes against Humanity

("Systematic-
Crimes against Humanity
"), an

over 21
year-long Canadian Judiciary-Driven Systemic-Racism

("Systemic-Racism),
an over 21 year-long Canadian Judiciary-Driven

Systemic-Incitement-of-discriminatory-hatred
("Systemic-Incitement-of-

discriminatory-hatred"), an over 21
year-long Canadian Judiciary-Driven

Systemic-Favouritism
("Systemic-Favouritism"), an over 21

year-long Canadian
Judiciary-Driven Systemic-
Obstruction of Justice
("Systemic-
Obstruction
of Justice
"), an over 21 year-long Canadian

Judiciary-Driven
Systematic-Torture ("Systematic-Torture").

B.        The Respondents, their Subordinates/Employees, Canadian
Lawyers, Canadian Judges, and their Canadian Co-Conspirator (Justice-)Officials,
Institutions, and entities had, against the Applicants and their Family,  ingloriously
and immorally Conspired also:

- in violation of
Rule I. 09
of the
Rules of
Civil Procedure

- in manners setout within
465.(1)
of the
Criminal
Code

- while defeating the purposes of
Section 80
of
the
Courts of Justice Act
.

- in a manner that violated and violates many of the
Applicants and their Family's rights through many Sections of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, inclusive of the Sections specified herein

- in a manner that violated and violates the
Human
Rights Code

also because:

i.          The Respondents, their Subordinates/Employees, Canadian Lawyers,
Canadian Judges, the Canadian Justice-System, and their Canadian Co-Conspirator
(Justice-)Officials, Institutions, and entities immorally Conspired against the
Applicants and their Family, also by,

a.         directing aforementioned Conspirators to immorally and pervertedly
torture innocent Disabled-Persons and their infant children for over 21 years
through abovementioned crimes

b.         directing aforementioned Conspirators to embezzle and appropriate
the futures of Canadian-Children other than the offspring of Canadian
Justice-Officials, and then, provide aforementioned futures to the offspring of
Canadian (Justice-)Officials through abovementioned crimes

c.         directing aforementioned Conspirators to immorally and
pervertedly divide & dissolve the Applicants' over 21 year-long
Legal-Matter with respect to abovementioned crimes (which initiated in 1988)
into illogical and meaningless pieces, pieces of which do not allow for the
Applicants to expose the evidences of a Gross
Chain Conspiracy
and
evidences of a Canadian Judiciary-Driven Systematic-Crime as setout within the
DC-08- 0074-ML file-numbered Affidavit of Ural Direk (made Attachment 1 to the
Notice of Constitutional Question. dated September 8th, 2009, served together with
this very Notice of Application), Affirmed Feb. 19
th
, 2009.

[
8
]

To some extent, the origins of the Direks'
complaints with the Ontario justice system are summarized in the following
excerpt from the endorsement of Bellamy J. in her April 30, 2007 decision
dismissing Ural's appeal from his 2004 convictions for uttering death threats
against two lawyers who had previously acted for him (
R. v. Direk
,

[2007] O.J. 1643 (S.C.J.) at paras. 2-4
):

2     The appellant [Ural Direk]
claims that for the last eighteen and a half years, there has existed in
Ontario a form of state corruption coupled with a massive conspiracy of fraud
and a gross conspiracy of silence against him. This has allegedly included
mental torture against him and his family, an assassination attempt by the
police and a police-led home invasion in which the police intentionally
destroyed evidence necessary for this appeal which would have exposed the
corruption. The appellant alleges that the "masterminds" and
participants in this conspiracy consist of a number of judges of the Court of
Appeal, at least two judges of the Superior Court of Justice, numerous lawyers
who have acted at various times for the appellant, the Law Society of Upper
Canada, at least one physician, the police generally, the officer-in-charge,
two court reporters who were compelled by the "masterminds" to issue
fraudulent transcripts in relation to this appeal, the Crown attorney who
prosecuted him, the lawyer who defended him (who herself was allegedly being
controlled by the "masterminds") and the trial judge who found him
guilty. Much of what was said about the above individuals, and in particular
about one of the lawyers who testified at the trial, would have been considered
defamatory had it been said outside the courtroom.

3     The appellant has had an
eighteen and a half year history with the legal system, which appears to have
started after he was injured in a motor vehicle accident in August 1988. He
instituted a law suit and later appealed the trial judge's findings.
Ultimately, McMurtry, C.J.O., Osborne and Abella, JJ.A. of the Ontario Court of
Appeal dismissed his appeal on June 3, 1998. The Supreme Court of Canada denied
him leave to appeal.

4     He evidently is most unhappy
with what he perceives as a grave injustice committed against him by the legal
system and has vociferously complained about his concerns to many people,
including Queen Elizabeth and the United Nations. He has regularly picketed a
number of courthouses and his lawyers' offices in downtown Toronto, and has
used a bullhorn to secure the public's attention to his concerns.

[
9
]

The Direks' Counter-Application is the latest
legal proceeding in which the Direks have sought a remedy for their complaints
regarding alleged corruption in Ontario's justice system.

Procedural Steps To Date

[
10
]

At an appearance before me not long after the
Direks served the Direks' Counter-Application, counsel for the AGO and the TPSB
advised that they intended to move under Rule 21 to stay or dismiss the Direks'
Counter-Application as against their respective clients. For the reasons
described below, numerous procedural delays have been encountered since that time,
and the motions only came on for argument on July 3, 2013.

[
11
]

As initially constituted, the Direks' Counter-Application
included as a co-applicant Ismet Direkoglu ("Ismet"), who is the
ex-wife of Ural and the mother of Ertug, Kemal and Elif. She lives on the
island of Cyprus. In the Direks' Counter-Application as initially issued, Ismet
was purportedly represented by Ural as her litigation guardian, under the
theory that she was a person under legal disability by reason of mental
illness.

[
12
]

Since the initial appearance on November 6,
2009, the parties have appeared before me on numerous occasions, in order to
address various procedural issues. To begin with, these appearances dealt with
the question of involvement of and representation for Ertug, Elif, and Ismet.
In a ruling released June 10, 2010 (the "June 10, 2010 Ruling") I
decided that, because they are not lawyers, Ural and Kemal could not act on
behalf of Ertug and Elif. I therefore directed that if Ertug and Elif wished to
continue as participants in the Direks' Counter-Application, they must attend
in court and represent themselves. Since that ruling, Ertug and Elif have
appeared on their own behalves only intermittently whenever these matters have
returned to court. Ural and Kemal have been present for all appearances.

[
13
]

The matter of the involvement of and
representation for Ismet was more complex in that Ural (who has been divorced
from Ismet for a number of years) purported to represent her as her litigation
guardian. Despite naming himself as Ismet's litigation guardian, Ural did not comply
with
rule 7.02
of the
Rules of Civil Procedure,
R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194,
in that he did not file an affidavit of litigation guardian nor did he retain a
lawyer to represent her interests.

[
14
]

The respondents, the AGO and the TPSB,
challenged the propriety of Ismet being a party to the Direks' Counter-Application. As a consequence, I
gave directions and set a timetable for the argument of a motion for the
determination of the question whether Ismet was under a legal disability and
whether she was a willing participant in the proceeding. I further gave
directions concerning service of notice of that motion and these proceedings on
Ismet in Cyprus so that she would be aware of the proceedings and thus be able
to respond and participate, if she chose to.

[
15
]

The motion regarding the status of Ismet as a
party to the Direks' Counter-Application was argued before me on June 4, 2010. In
the June 10, 2010 Ruling, I concluded as follows:

(a)

based upon current medical evidence (including a
medical report obtained by the Direks themselves from Ismet’s treating
psychiatrist in Cyprus) Ismet is not currently under any legal disability;

(b)

having received notice of the proceedings and
not being under any legal disability, Ismet has stated through a lawyer in
Cyprus that she does not wish to be included as a co-applicant or have any
other involvement in these proceedings; and

(c)

as a consequence, Ismet should be removed as a
co-applicant.

I directed the parties to return to me for
purposes of fixing a timetable for further steps in the AGO Application and Direks'
Counter-Application and also to address the subject of the costs of the motion
involving the status of Ismet.

[
16
]

On June 21, 2010 the Direks served a motion for
leave to appeal the June 10, 2010 Ruling to the Divisional Court. A stated
ground for that motion was that "The Honourable Mr. Justice D.G.
Stinson had, against the Applicants [the Direks] a severe conflict of interest
and conspired, under subsection 465.(1) of the
Criminal Code
of Canada,
with His Honour's Co-Conspirators in a manner in which does, pursuant to
Clause
62.02(4)
(a) of the
Rules of Civil Procedure
,
warrant the granting of
leave sought herein."

[
17
]

The Direks' motion for leave to appeal the June
10, 2010 Ruling was ultimately heard and dismissed by Ferrier J. on December
20, 2010.

[
18
]

Meanwhile, the Direks brought a motion to have
me recuse myself. In reasons released December 13, 2010, I refused that motion.
The Direks sought leave to appeal that decision. Their leave motion was denied
by Swinton J. on March 31, 2011.

[
19
]

The Direks then brought motions to have the
decisions of Ferrier J. dated December 20, 2010 and Swinton J. dated March 31, 2011
reviewed by a panel of the Divisional Court. On June 17, 2011, Aston J.
quashed those motions and dismissed the appeals.

[
20
]

Subsequently, the AGO and the TPSB brought a
motion pursuant to rule 37.16 for an order prohibiting the Direks from making
further motions in these proceedings in both the Superior Court of Justice and
the Divisional Court without leave of a judge. That relief was granted by Dambrot
J. in a decision released November 1, 2011 (reported at
2011 ONSC 6375
).

[
21
]

In most, if not all of the foregoing judicial determinations, the
Direks were ordered to pay costs to their successful opponents. There is no
evidence before me that they have satisfied any of those costs awards.

[
22
]

The net result of the foregoing procedural
journey is that no substantive progress was made between November 2009 and
November 2011 in relation to either the AGO Application or the Direks' Counter-
Application. The matters then lay dormant for a period of time until the AGO
and the TPSB requested that I schedule a timetable for the argument of their Rule
21 motions. After several months of delay, I imposed a timetable, the result of
which was the argument of the motions before me on July 3, 2013.

The Direks' Counter-Application

[
23
]

In support of their motions to stay or dismiss
the Direks' Counter-Application, the AGO and the TPSB relied only on the
contents of the Notice of Application issued by the Direks in the Direks' Counter-Application,
the Notice of Application issued by AGO in the AGO Application, and certain
previous orders made in the proceedings. In response to the motions to dismiss,
the Direks filed a lengthy responding motion record including an affidavit of Ural
and Kemal dated January 30, 2013 (the "Direks' Affidavit”). The Direks' Affidavit

I have reproduced at length (and verbatim) the
foregoing single paragraph from the Direks’ 125 page affidavit to provide an
indication regarding the nature and scope of the allegations made by them. In
their affidavit, they affirm that these allegations are true.

[
25
]

In essence, the complaints by the Direks are
based upon their assertion and belief that they are the victims of a "24
year long Canadian Judiciary Driven Gross Systemic
Chain Conspiracy
”
involving the Ontario justice system, the Ontario Government "High-Authoritative
Jewish Figures, the Attorney General of Ontario" and others. The named
participants in this alleged conspiracy include, among
others, over 16 lawyers, 18 trial judges, 8 judges of
the Court of Appeal (two of whom are now judges of the Supreme Court of Canada),
multiple law firms, legal assistants, court reporters, a FedEx courier, the
Toronto Community Housing Corporation, the Ministry of Community and Social
Services, the Community Care Access Center, the Information and Privacy Commissioner,
several other justice officials, 5 doctors (3 in Ontario and 2 in Cyprus), and
a utility company. The Direks accuse all these parties of being participants in
a fraudulent conspiracy in the manner set out in
s. 122
of the
Criminal Code
,
s. 341 of the
Criminal Code
, s.361.1 of the
Criminal Code
and s. 465.1
of the
Criminal Code
. Among other acts of conspiracy, the Direks allege
that there was a fraudulent attempt to make it appear that Ismet does not have
a legal disability; that Ismet was sexually abused and impregnated in Cyprus by
an agent of the AGO; that the listed parties have conspired to fraudulently
indicate that Ismet does not want to participate in the proceedings; and that
the listed parties are obstructing the Direks from "receiving their receiving
their legally-entitled relief of … Four-Billion Dollars ($4,000,000,000.00)”.

The Rule 21 Motions

[
26
]

The moving parties rely on, among other grounds,

rule 21.01(3)
(c) of the
Rules of Civil Procedure
. That provision allows
a judge to stay or dismiss an action where it is “frivolous, vexatious or
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court.” Although proceedings commenced
by notice of application are not expressly mentioned in rule 21.01(3)(c),
through the use of rule 1.04(2) and the inherent jurisdiction of the court to
control its own processes, I hold that a rule 21.01(3)(c) motion may be used to
challenge the propriety of a proceeding commenced in that fashion. To hold
otherwise would impose an overly restrictive approach to the ability of the
court to weed out specious litigation.

[
27
]

I appreciate that the Direks are
self-represented and have not had legal advice or assistance in preparing their
materials. That said, they have chosen to initiate a court proceeding, in which
they have made serious allegations against numerous parties. It is no
overstatement to describe the Direks’ multiple allegations of fraud, criminal
conspiracy, obstruction of justice and commission of crimes against humanity by
the various parties listed as outlandish, offensive and outrageous. To quote
Dambrot J. in his decision prohibiting further motions by the Direks in these
proceedings, the allegations are “bizarre, scandalous and vexatious.” (
2011
ONSC 6375
at para.
5
). On their face, the allegations are patently incredible
and unbelievable. To suggest that such a wide ranging collection of
individuals, public officeholders and agencies have somehow engaged in a
conspiracy to deprive the Direks of remedies for their legal rights strains
credulity past the breaking point. While I am conscious of the principle that,
generally speaking, at the stage of a motion to strike, claims made must be
taken as capable of proof, that principle should not be taken to permit a party
to continue to advance absurd allegations. In this case, put simply, the Direks'
allegations are not worthy of belief. As such, the Direks' Counter-Application
has no reasonable prospect of success.

[
28
]

The courts and the civil justice system exist to
provide members of our society with the means by which they can resolve disputes
by seeking remedies and redress for their legitimate claims. As the Supreme
Court of Canada stated in
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc
.
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959
(S.C.C.) at 970, the rules empowering judges to stay or dismiss proceedings
without legal merit were “derived from the courts’ power to ensure both that
they remained a forum in which genuine legal issues were addressed and that
they did not become a vehicle for vexatious actions without legal merit
designed solely to harass another party.”

[
29
]

In
R v. Rose,

1998 CanLII 768 (SCC)
, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 262 at para

131
, the Supreme Court quoted with approval Professor I. H. Jacob in “The Inherent
Jurisdiction of the Court” (1970), 23 Current Legal Problems at page 27, as
follows:

…[T]he essential character of a
superior court of law necessarily involves that it should be invested with a
power to maintain its authority and to prevent its process being obstructed and
abused. Such a power is intrinsic in a superior court; it is its very
life-blood, its very essence, its imminent attribute. Without such a power, the
court would have form but would lack substance. The jurisdiction which is inherent
in a superior court of law is that which enables it to fulfill in itself as a
court of law. The juridical basis of this jurisdiction is therefore the
authority of the judiciary to uphold, to protect and to fulfill the judicial
function of administering justice according to law in a regular, orderly and
effective manner.”

[
30
]

In
R v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd
.,

2011 SCC 42
at paras.
19 and 20
the Supreme Court again addressed the goals of
the power to strike out claims that have no reasonable prospect of success:

19        The power to strike out
claims that have no reasonable prospect of success is a valuable housekeeping
measure essential to effective and fair litigation. In it unclutters the
proceedings, weeding out the hopeless claims and ensuring that those that have
some chance of success go on to trial.

20        This promotes two goods
-- efficiency in the conduct of the litigation and correct results. The
striking out claims that have no reasonable prospect of success promotes
litigation efficiency, reducing time and cost. The litigants can focus on
serious claims, without devoting days and sometimes weeks of evidence and
argument to claims that are in any event hopeless. The same applies to judges
and juries, whose attention is focused where it should be -- on claims that
have a reasonable chance of success. The efficiency gained by weeding out on
meritorious claims in turn contributes to better justice. The more the evidence
and arguments are trained on the real issues, the more likely it is that the
trial process will successfully come to grips with the parties’ respective
positions on those issues and the merits of the case.

[
31
]

The allegations advanced by the Direks in the Direks'
Counter-Application are, in my respectful view, so outlandish and incredible
that they are hopeless and have no prospect of success. To consume the
resources of the court and the responding parties in permitting the Direks to
pursue their requested “six month incessant initial-continuation of the
November 6, 2009 hearing” would be an abuse of process. To permit such a
proceeding to unfold for no proper or productive purpose would bring the
administration of justice into disrepute; in turn, were I to allow it to
continue I would be derelict in my duty to fulfill the judicial function of administering
justice in an orderly and effective manner.

[
32
]

It is conceivable that somewhere in the mass of
largely unintelligible material filed by the Direks, there is some information
or complaint that warrants the attention of the court. As currently constituted,
however, the Direks' Counter-Application is founded on allegations that cannot
conceivably succeed. As a result, the Rule 21 motions must be granted and the Direks'
Counter-Application must be permanently stayed.

[
33
]

To the extent the Direks assert a claim to the
property that was seized by the police and which is subject to the AGO Application
under the
Civil Remedies Act
, it remains open to them to respond to the AGO
Application by tendering evidence that properly addresses the issues raised in
that proceeding. To the extent they wish to advance a proper claim for other
relief, they remain at liberty to do so in a proceeding that is correctly
constituted and pleaded; such liberty is, of course, subject to any defences
that may be raised to such claims (including the expiration of any applicable
limitation periods) as well as any application or motion that may be brought
pursuant to s. 140 of the
Courts of Justice Act,
or the
Rules
,
or otherwise.

Disposition

[
34
]

For these reasons, the moving parties’ Rule 21
motions are granted and the Direks' Counter-Application is permanently stayed.
